solutions.check: 33 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: What fun for different Labour leader to get in charge!

definitions.note: a phrase naming the thing that is fun, so it stands for a noun

indicators.note: different asks for the word for in a different arrangement of its letters
a leader is at the front, so only the opening letter of Labour is used

parts.note: the first letter of Labour

explanation.surface: A sarcastic cheer at the prospect of yet another new Labour leader taking charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' looks like a politician, but 'leader' takes just the first letter of Labour. 'different' rearranges FOR into FRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A frolic is a playful, lively bit of amusement, so it is fun.

clue.text: In brief, Rees-Mogg on the house

indicators.note: In says the answer is sitting inside the words that follow rather than being built out of them.

parts.note: the letters run across the join, the f closing brief and ree opening Rees

explanation.surface: A quick word about Rees-Mogg, drinking at the establishment's expense.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Rees-Mogg is the tweed-and-Latin Tory MP, and the hyphenated name makes the hiding place look like a person rather than a string of letters. 'In brief' pretends to promise an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink on the house is paid for by the bar rather than the drinker, which is to say it costs nothing.

clue.text: (& 15/23dn.)Mates turned up with delight for old-fashioned foreplay

indicators.note: In a down entry something turned up is stood on its head, so its letters are read from the bottom.

parts.note: mates are pals, and this entry runs downwards so pals is read upwards
with and and both set one thing alongside another
to delight someone is to please them, as in being '___ pink'

explanation.surface: Friends who have arrived thrilled at the prospect of some dated courting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delight' is the verb tickle, not the noun, which is why it looks like a state of mind. The phrase belongs to the era of seaside postcards and has been quaint for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Slap and tickle is the old British phrase for amorous fumbling, dated enough now that the clue can call it old-fashioned.

clue.text: An old president needs good wife and coach to get hard

parts.note: g is the standard short form for good
w is the standard short form for wife
a coach is a bus built for long journeys
h is the standard short form for hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.surface: A former president who wants a decent wife and a trainer before he can toughen up.
explanation.walkthrough: George W Bush was US president from 2001 to 2009, and the middle initial is what everybody called him by. 'Hard' is the H on the side of a pencil.
explanation.definitionFit: Bush left the White House in 2009, so he is a president in the former sense that 'old' carries here.

clue.text: Squadron leader with automatic makes mark?

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so only that one comes away.

parts.note: the front letter of squadron
an automatic is a car that changes its own gears

explanation.surface: An RAF officer with a pistol, leaving his mark on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Squadron leader is a real RAF rank, which is why the phrase reads as a man rather than a letter, and an automatic in the same breath sounds like the gun he is carrying. It is the car on the forecourt.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the mark left on the skin once a wound has healed over.

clue.text: Foot's area: toeing the party line?

definitions.meaning: the part of the body the answer names, read as one word
the marching sense, which needs the answer split into two words

explanation.surface: A politician's patch of territory and his obedience to the party whip.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot is capitalised to pull in Michael Foot, Labour's leader in the early 1980s, when the clue wants the thing on the end of your leg. The second definition splits the answer where the first does not.
explanation.definitionFit: The instep is the arched upper surface of the foot between toes and ankle; read as two words, being in step with a party is marching exactly to its line.

clue.text: Bear down on English far right figure?

parts.note: Rupert Bear is the check-trousered bear of the Daily Express cartoon strip
low is what down means of a level or a position
e is the standard short form for English

explanation.surface: A bear advancing menacingly on some right-wing Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear down on' reads as one phrase and is really three separate instructions. Rupert Lowe is the Great Yarmouth MP elected for Nigel Farage's Reform UK and since estranged from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowe sits at the far right of British politics, so naming him is defining the type by one example, which the question mark admits.

clue.text: It takes one tit to break into China's future capability

indicators.note: Breaking a thing leaves its pieces loose, and loose letters can be set down in a new order.
Into names the word the broken letters are pushed inside, which splits apart to take them.

parts.note: china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, so a china is a pal
the six letters of one tit, reset before they go in

explanation.surface: Only an idiot would try to force a way into the Chinese market.
explanation.walkthrough: A tit here is a fool rather than a bird, and china for a mate comes from the Cockney rhyme china plate. 'It takes one to know one' is the phrase the opening borrows.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential is what somebody could do rather than what they have done, so it is capability still waiting on the future.

clue.text: Sex primarily has the power to probe

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes before all else, so the letter wanted is the one at the front.

parts.note: the opening letter of sex
someone who can do a thing has the power to do it

explanation.surface: Sex, above all else, is what gives a person the power to probe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has the power to' looks like a phrase built to hold the sentence together and is the whole second half of the wordplay. Can is the plain verb of ability.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan something is to run over it looking for what it holds, which is what probing it means.

clue.text: Reform moving to left — "Why?" texted earlier

indicators.note: A thing that is moving is no longer where it was put, so the letters end up in new places.
A word texted is written the short way a phone message writes it, the whole word shrunk to the letter that sounds like it.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
l is the standard short form for left
y is the single letter a text message puts for why

explanation.surface: Reform UK drifting leftwards, and an earlier text message asking why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' looks like an instruction to re-form something and is in fact the fodder; 'moving' is the instruction. The party is Nigel Farage's Reform UK, and a right-wing party heading left is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: What happened formerly happened at an earlier time, so either word drops into the same sentence unchanged.

clue.text: With the light on, male does not get stiff

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a verb phrase, but a body that never sets rigid is exactly what the adjective describes.

parts.note: a lamp that is on is lit
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man who cannot rise to the occasion with the lamp still burning.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude reading of 'does not get stiff' is the one the surface wants, and the answer takes it literally, as a body that stays supple. 'With the light on' is the past participle lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lithe bends easily and never sets rigid, which is what refusing to get stiff amounts to.

clue.text: Elon Musk's heavenly body? Cold arse!

parts.note: Pluto is the dwarf planet, and the question mark allows it as one heavenly body among many
c is the standard short form for cold, the letter on a tap
both are what you call a man you have no time for

explanation.surface: Elon Musk's physique appraised, and dismissed as a chilly backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Naming Musk defines the type by one example, which is what makes the clue a jab rather than a dictionary entry. Pluto was demoted from planet to dwarf planet in 2006, and the question mark concedes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is someone whose money buys political power, the charge routinely levelled at Musk.

clue.text: Jail like Tulsa lacking centre for game

parts.note: the can is slang for prison
as and like both introduce a comparison

indicators.note: A word lacking its centre keeps only what sits at either end of it.

parts.note: the first and last letters of Tulsa, with uls gone from the middle

explanation.surface: Imprisonment in a Tulsa that has lost its city centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Canasta is the two-pack rummy game that swept Britain in the 1950s. 'Can' for jail is American prison slang, which is why an American city keeps it company.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a card game for two to six players, so 'game' is the plain category it belongs to.

clue.text: Course programme, organised bullshit, say — hit out

indicators.note: Organising a heap means setting its contents in a fresh arrangement, which is what these letters get.
Out means gone from the mix, so the letters just named are dropped before anything else happens.

parts.note: the eleven letters the wordplay starts from
these three letters are lifted out of that heap before it is shuffled

explanation.surface: A course programme built from tidied-up nonsense, and someone lashing out.
explanation.walkthrough: The deletion happens before the shuffle, so 'hit' has to be found in the fodder rather than in the answer. 'Say' is part of the letters here, not the usual for-example marker.
explanation.definitionFit: A syllabus is the document setting out what a course will cover, which is its programme of study.

clue.text: see 3dn.
A joint before sex, rather excited — act badly

parts.note: a ham is a joint of meat
it is the coy old word for sex
someone up for something is roused and keen

explanation.surface: Smoking a joint before going to bed with someone, thoroughly worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' is the spliff in the surface and the Sunday roast in the wordplay. 'It' for sex is the 1920s usage that gave Clara Bow her name as the It Girl.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham it up is to overact, piling on gestures until the performance is bad on purpose.

clue.text: One who makes little pricks beat one way

parts.note: a tattoo is a drumbeat, as at a military tattoo
i is the Roman numeral for one, and this is the clue's second one, not the one that opens it
st is the short form of street, a kind of way

explanation.surface: Somebody who gets small-time idiots beaten in one particular fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prick' is the insult in the surface and the needle's puncture in the definition. A tattoo was originally the drum signal calling soldiers back to quarters for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattooist works by driving a needle in and out thousands of times, so the trade really is making little pricks.

clue.text: Clinton's reckoning

definitions.meaning: the president taken by his first name rather than his surname
the account presented when something has to be paid for

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton facing a day of reckoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is nothing more than 'is', which is what lets three words read as a sentence. Bill Clinton was US president from 1993 to 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinton is named by his given name, Bill; and a bill is the reckoning the waiter brings once the meal is over.

clue.text: US bloke getting end away — failure

indicators.note: Getting something away is getting rid of it, and the end of a word is its last letter.

parts.note: dude is the American word for a bloke
the last letter of dude, and the one sent away

explanation.surface: An American man having a successful night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting your end away' is British slang for having sex, and that is the whole of the surface; the wordplay reads the same words letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud is a shell that never goes off or a gadget that never works, so it is a failure in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Who'll cure fish on the turn

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun, naming the man by the one thing he is there to do.

indicators.note: Something on the turn is going round the other way, so the letters are read back to front.

parts.note: the fish is a cod, and it is read backwards

explanation.surface: Fish that is starting to go off, and the man who will make you better.
explanation.walkthrough: Fish 'on the turn' is fish going off, which is the picture the surface paints while the same phrase tells the solver to read the fish backwards. Doc is the familiar short form of doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A doc is a doctor, and curing the sick is the job the definition names him by.

clue.text: Balls on a roll

parts.note: balls and rot are both ways of saying that what was just said is nonsense
the article supplies its own letter

explanation.surface: Someone talking nonsense while enjoying a run of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a roll' is one idiom in the surface and two separate jobs in the clue. Balls and rot belong to the same register, which is what makes the swap invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is a roll in the old sense of a written list of names, the sense that survives in 'roll call'.

clue.text: Damn recruiting ex-VP to steady the ship?

indicators.note: Recruiting somebody takes them into the ranks, so the letters named are taken inside.

parts.note: blast is the mild curse that damn covers
Al Gore was vice-president under Clinton, and his first name is what goes in

explanation.surface: A swear word signing up a former vice-president to keep things on an even keel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ballast is the weight carried low in a hull to stop a vessel rolling, so 'steady the ship' names the job rather than offering a synonym. Al Gore served two terms as vice-president.
explanation.definitionFit: To ballast a vessel is to weight her down until she sits steady, which is steadying the ship.

clue.text: He scored, though half pissed

indicators.note: half means keep only one of the two composers in the slang phrase and drop the rest

parts.note: Brahms and Liszt is Cockney rhyming slang for pissed, meaning drunk
the second half of the slang phrase, 'and Liszt', which is discarded

explanation.surface: Someone scored, even though they were halfway drunk at the time.
explanation.walkthrough: In British rhyming slang 'Brahms and Liszt' means pissed (drunk); half of that pair is Brahms. 'scored' is the composer's sense, writing a musical score, not the sexual or sporting one.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Brahms was a composer, so he scored music, writing orchestral scores.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Cause unnecessary alarm about extremely randy Casanova

parts.note: c is short for circa, the about that goes in front of a date

indicators.note: The extremes of a word are the letters at its two far ends, and only those are wanted.

parts.note: the outermost letters of randy
a wolf is a man who chases women, which is what Casanova's name stands for

explanation.surface: Raising a needless alarm about a thoroughly randy seducer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the preposition the alarm is raised about and is the circa abbreviation. The phrase comes from Aesop's shepherd boy, who shouted wolf until nobody came.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry wolf is to raise an alarm when nothing is wrong, which is unnecessary alarm and the reason the next one is ignored.

clue.text: Tense, vulgar swearing online? True, sadly

parts.note: fu is how the two-word obscenity gets typed in a comment thread

indicators.note: Something done sadly has gone wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are no longer in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: Coarse abuse posted on the internet which is, sadly, accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' opens the clue looking like a description of the mood and is the grammar term. Past, present and future are the three the answer belongs among.
explanation.definitionFit: The future is one of the tenses an English verb takes, so naming a tense can name this one.

clue.text: Broadcaster Widdecombe, catty creature on right?

parts.note: Ann Widdecombe, the former Conservative minister who later stood for Reform UK
the ounce is the snow leopard, which is a cat
r is the standard short form for right

explanation.surface: Ann Widdecombe billed as a broadcaster, next to a spiteful animal of the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is the snow leopard, a crossword regular whose name has nothing to do with weight. 'Catty' does the same double work, meaning spiteful on the surface and feline underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: An announcer is the voice that reads the news or introduces the programmes, which is a kind of broadcaster.

clue.text: Wally's dinner date centre

indicators.note: The centre of a phrase is what sits at its middle, so the letters taken are the ones with as much either side of them.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across the words

explanation.surface: A fool at the very centre of his own evening out.
explanation.walkthrough: Wally is British for a fool, the playground word the seaside postcards kept going. The letters straddle two words, which is why the join is easy to read past.
explanation.definitionFit: A wally is British slang for someone socially hopeless, which is what calling a man a nerd says about him.

clue.text: Said "squeeze tightly", as a token of love

indicators.note: Said points at the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so what is wanted is what the ear hears.

parts.note: to wring a cloth is to squeeze it tightly, and its w falls silent when the word is spoken

explanation.surface: An instruction to hold something very tight, offered as a sign of affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Wring is what you do to a wet towel, and its opening w is never sounded, so the two words are one noise. The definition is the engagement ring, not the boxing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring is the thing given and worn to show that somebody is loved and spoken for, at an engagement or a wedding.

clue.text: Steer clear of sexist term!

definitions.meaning: the verb, going round the edge of something rather than through it
the noun, an old leering word for a woman

explanation.surface: A warning to avoid an offensive piece of vocabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue tells you to avoid a sexist term and the answer is one, which is the whole joke. 'A bit of skirt' is the phrase the second definition is reaching for.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt something is to go round its edge rather than through it; and skirt for a woman is the dated slang the clue calls sexist.

clue.text: Some of us ignore a two-fingered salute?

indicators.note: Some of a phrase is a part of it, so the answer is a run of letters lifted out whole.

parts.note: the letters run from the end of us into the start of ignore

explanation.surface: A few of us pretending not to notice a rude gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-fingered salute is the British V-sign, palm turned inwards, and it is one gesture among many, which the question mark concedes. 'Some of us' reads as a group of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-fingered salute says something without words, which is what a sign does — this one rudely.

clue.text: "Heard Carney's a major commie!"

indicators.note: Heard means taken in by ear, so the spelling that counts is the one the sound suggests.

parts.note: Carney is Mark Carney, Canada's prime minister, and his first name with the clue's s said aloud is the surname wanted

explanation.surface: Somebody overhearing that Mark Carney is a leading communist.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Carney ran the Bank of England before becoming Canada's prime minister, and calling a central banker a communist is the joke. The possessive s is what supplies the sound of the x.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Marx wrote the Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital, so no commie is more major than him.

clue.text: Party that's enduring disastrous rating hell

indicators.note: A disaster leaves everything in the wrong place, and letters in the wrong places have to be set down afresh.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A political party living through a catastrophic slump in the opinion polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' is the political one in the surface and the drinking one in the answer. Ratings hell is what a collapse in the polls gets called, which is why the fodder reads as plain English.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-nighter is a party that runs until morning, so it is the one still going long after the rest have stopped.
